title: Billing It Right: CPT/HCPCS, Panel Codes, Medical Necessity and the ABN
summary: Learn how a laboratory claim pairs a CPT/HCPCS procedure code with an ICD-10-CM diagnosis, why the panel code must be billed when every panel test is performed, what makes upcoding and unbundling improper, and when Medicare requires an Advance Beneficiary Notice.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 13 Hits 4, 6 and 9, Exam Traps 1 and 6, and the “Do not confuse” comparison (Exam Traps item 7, its Table 2 and the closing line, item 8). Checked against the CMS HCPCS page, the 2026 NCCI Policy Manual (Chapters I and X), the OIG Compliance Program Guidance for Clinical Laboratories (63 FR 45076, 1998), 31 U.S.C. 3729, 42 CFR 410.32, 411.15, 411.404 and 411.408, 45 CFR 162.1002, and the CMS ABN page and form instructions. The reviewer calls up-coding and unbundling “illegal fraud” without qualification; the sources tie fraud liability to knowing conduct (rv-upcoding-knowing). The reviewer’s ABN dodge omits that routine or blanket ABNs are not acceptable (rv-abn-routine). Not taught as fact: the “A–V” letter range for Level II codes, the PSA codes 84153 and G0103 and the PSA-with-heart-failure example (replaced by the CMS lipid-panel example), the 72-hour rule, DRG/APC payment, capitation, leases, budgeting and the CLIA competency schedule. US Medicare rules only.

objectives: Distinguish HCPCS Level I (CPT) from HCPCS Level II codes and from ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes.
Apply the panel-code rule and define unbundling and upcoding.
State when and how an Advance Beneficiary Notice is given for a test that may not be medically necessary.

scenes.title: Three billing shortcuts
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: an outpatient Medicare claim is being prepared. (1) Cholesterol, triglycerides and HDL cholesterol were ordered as three separate tests and performed together; the billing clerk plans three separate codes. (2) A vitamin D test arrived with a diagnosis that may not support it; the clerk suggests swapping in a diagnosis code that “usually gets paid”. (3) To be safe, the clerk wants every outpatient to sign a blank ABN at registration. Question token: “Which shortcut is allowed?”

cues.text: A Medicare outpatient claim is being prepared. Cholesterol, triglycerides and HDL were ordered separately and run together, and the clerk plans three separate codes.
A vitamin D order came with a diagnosis that may not support it, so the clerk wants to swap in a diagnosis that usually gets paid, and to have every patient sign a blank waiver at registration.
Which of these shortcuts is allowed?

scenes.title: Two code sets on every claim
scenes.altText: Schematic claim form with two boxes. WHAT box: HCPCS (Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System) has two levels. Level I is CPT (Current Procedural Terminology), a numeric system maintained by the American Medical Association; CPT codes are 5 numeric digits and are updated yearly. Level II codes are alphanumeric, a single letter followed by 4 numeric digits, maintained by CMS, for products, supplies and services not in CPT. WHY box: diagnoses are coded in ICD-10-CM, the HIPAA standard code set for diseases and conditions since October 1, 2015 (45 CFR 162.1002). Clinical laboratory tests are named in the standard as services coded with HCPCS and CPT.

cues.text: A Medicare lab claim pairs two kinds of code. The procedure code says what was done; the diagnosis code says why.
Procedure codes come from HCPCS, which has two levels. Level one is CPT, maintained by the American Medical Association: five numeric digits, updated every year.
Level two is maintained by CMS: a single letter followed by four digits, for items and services that CPT does not describe.
Diagnoses are coded in ICD-10-CM, the US standard code set since October 2015.

scenes.title: One panel, one code
scenes.altText: Correct-coding card (CMS NCCI Policy Manual 2026): report the most comprehensive HCPCS/CPT code that describes the services; do not report several codes when one comprehensive code describes them (unbundling). Panel card: if all tests of a CPT-defined organ or disease panel are performed, bill the panel code, even when the tests were ordered individually; example: cholesterol 82465 + triglycerides 84478 + HDL cholesterol 83718 = lipid panel 80061. NCCI edits pair each panel code with its component codes. A component repeated on the same day may be reported separately only when medically reasonable and necessary, with a modifier. Upcoding card: a code may be reported only if all services it describes were performed. Liability card: the OIG warns that intentional or knowing upcoding could violate the False Claims Act and other civil and criminal law; under the Act, “knowingly” includes deliberate ignorance and reckless disregard and requires no proof of specific intent to defraud.

cues.text: Correct coding means reporting the single most comprehensive code that describes the work. Splitting it into component codes is unbundling.

For laboratories, that means panels. If every test in a CPT-defined panel is performed, bill the panel code, even if the tests were ordered one by one: cholesterol, triglycerides and HDL become one lipid panel code.
Upcoding is the mirror image: billing a code whose services were not all performed.

The HHS Office of Inspector General warns that knowing upcoding can violate the False Claims Act, and under that law, reckless disregard counts as knowing. No proof of specific intent to defraud is needed.

scenes.title: Medical necessity and the ABN
scenes.altText: Necessity card: Medicare excludes services that are not reasonable and necessary for the diagnosis or treatment of illness or injury (42 CFR 411.15(k)(1)); a diagnostic lab test must be ordered by the practitioner treating the patient who uses the result (410.32(a)); the ordering practitioner documents medical necessity, and the billing lab keeps the diagnostic information it received (410.32(d)(2)). OIG: coverage policies may limit a test to specific diagnoses; labs must not invent diagnoses, reuse earlier ones, or auto-insert codes, and should ask the ordering practitioner instead. ABN card (CMS-R-131): when Medicare is not likely to cover a specific test, deliver the Advance Beneficiary Notice BEFORE the service, early enough for an informed choice; the patient chooses and signs; keep a signed copy; never required in emergencies. Routine or blanket notices are not acceptable. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Medicare pays only for services that are reasonable and necessary to diagnose or treat the patient. The treating practitioner orders the test and documents why; the lab keeps the diagnostic information it received.
The lab must never invent or swap a diagnosis to get paid. If information is missing, it asks the ordering practitioner.

If Medicare is not likely to pay for a specific test, the patient gets an Advance Beneficiary Notice before the test, in time to decide. The signed copy is kept. Blanket notices for everyone are not acceptable, and none is needed in an emergency.

Back to the hook: bill the lipid panel code, keep the ordered diagnosis and ask the practitioner, and give a specific notice only when there is a real reason to expect denial. None of the three shortcuts is allowed.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Up-coding and unbundling are clever billing optimizations” (✓ they are improper coding; done knowingly, they create False Claims Act liability); “The tests were ordered separately, so bill them separately” (✓ if every test of a CPT panel is performed, report the panel code); “Fix a denial by changing the diagnosis, or have everyone sign an ABN” (✓ the diagnosis comes from the ordering practitioner; the ABN is specific, given before the test, and not routine).

cues.text: Trap one: upcoding and unbundling are smart billing. No: they are improper coding, and knowingly submitting such a false claim creates liability under the False Claims Act.
Trap two: separately ordered tests are billed separately. No: when every test in a panel is performed, the panel code is billed.
Trap three: fix a likely denial by changing the diagnosis, or by giving everyone a waiver. No: ask the ordering practitioner, and give a specific notice before the test only when denial is likely.

scenes.title: What, why, warn before
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Code WHAT, code WHY, warn BEFORE: the CPT/HCPCS code says WHAT was done, the ICD-10-CM code says WHY, and the ABN warns BEFORE the test. One panel, one code.” Tokens: WHAT = CPT/HCPCS · WHY = ICD-10-CM · BEFORE = ABN. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: code what, code why, warn before. The procedure code says what was done, the diagnosis code says why, and the notice warns the patient before the test. And one panel, one code.

Where it breaks: the panel code applies only when every component is performed; a medically necessary repeat of a component can be billed separately with a modifier; no notice is needed in an emergency; and these are Medicare rules, so other payers may differ.

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “WHAT = CPT (HCPCS Level I, AMA, 5 digits) or HCPCS Level II (CMS, letter + 4 digits) · WHY = ICD-10-CM”, “All panel tests done → panel code · no upcoding · ABN before the test, specific, not routine”.

cues.text: Bill the single code that matches the work, using the panel code whenever every panel test was done, take the diagnosis only from the ordering practitioner, and give a specific Advance Beneficiary Notice before the test when Medicare is likely to deny it.

All panel tests → panel code · no upcoding · specific ABN first

explanation.what: Plain language: a lab bill says what test was done and why. Use the one code that truly matches the work, take the reason from the doctor who ordered it, and warn the patient in writing beforehand if Medicare will probably not pay. Scientific terms: HCPCS Level I (CPT, AMA, 5 numeric digits), HCPCS Level II (CMS, one letter + 4 digits), ICD-10-CM, organ/disease-oriented panel, NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits, unbundling, upcoding, False Claims Act, reasonable and necessary (42 CFR 411.15(k)), Advance Beneficiary Notice of Noncoverage (ABN, Form CMS-R-131).
explanation.why: Payment depends on codes, so codes that overstate the work (upcoding) or split a comprehensive service into its parts (unbundling) lead to inappropriate payment, which NCCI edits are designed to prevent; a claim submitted knowingly false (including in reckless disregard) creates False Claims Act liability. Medicare pays only for reasonable and necessary services, so the diagnosis supplied by the ordering practitioner documents medical necessity, and some coverage policies limit a test to specific diagnoses, and the ABN lets the patient decide, before the test, whether to accept financial liability.
explanation.measure: CPT: 5 numeric digits (AMA, yearly). HCPCS Level II: 1 letter + 4 digits (CMS). ICD-10-CM: diagnoses since October 1, 2015. Panel: all component tests performed → panel code (cholesterol 82465 + triglycerides 84478 + HDL 83718 → lipid panel 80061). ABN: written, specific test and reason, before the service, signed copy kept, not routine, not in emergencies.
explanation.differs: Upcoding (a code describing more than was done) vs unbundling (component codes instead of one comprehensive code) vs correct panel billing; coding error vs knowing false claim; procedure code (what) vs diagnosis code (why); specific ABN vs blanket notice.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the correct code for a set of tests that make up a panel, identify upcoding vs unbundling, choose the HCPCS level from a code format, or decide what the lab must do when Medicare may deny a test for medical necessity.

questions.stem: A physician separately orders cholesterol, triglycerides and HDL cholesterol for a Medicare outpatient, and the laboratory performs all three on the same specimen. How should the tests be billed?

options.rationale: Correct. When all tests of a CPT-defined panel are performed, the NCCI manual requires the panel code, even if the tests were ordered individually.

options.text: With the three individual test codes, because they were ordered separately
options.rationale: Incorrect. Reporting the component codes instead of the panel code is unbundling.

options.text: With the panel code plus the three individual codes
options.rationale: Incorrect. NCCI edits pair the panel code with its components; a component may be added only for a medically necessary repeat, with a modifier.

options.text: With whichever combination of codes pays the most
options.rationale: Incorrect. Codes must describe the service performed; choosing codes to maximise payment is improper and, if knowing, can violate the False Claims Act.

questions.stem: A code consisting of a single letter followed by four numeric digits, maintained by CMS, belongs to which code set?

options.rationale: Correct. CMS maintains Level II alphanumeric codes for items and services not described by CPT.
Incorrect. CPT codes are 5 numeric digits maintained by the AMA.
Incorrect. ICD-10-CM is the diagnosis code set (why a test was done), not a procedure code set.
Incorrect. NCCI edits are pairs of existing HCPCS/CPT codes, not a separate code set.

questions.stem: A Medicare outpatient’s test order carries a diagnosis for which Medicare is likely to deny the test as not reasonable and necessary. What should happen?

options.text: Before testing, give the patient a written ABN naming the test and the reason payment is likely to be denied, and keep the signed copy
options.rationale: Correct. The ABN must be specific, delivered before the service in time for an informed choice, and retained.

options.text: Replace the diagnosis with one that is usually covered
options.rationale: Incorrect. Labs must not create or substitute diagnosis information; they ask the ordering practitioner.

options.text: Have every outpatient sign a blank ABN at registration
options.rationale: Incorrect. Blank or routine notices are not acceptable evidence of advance notice.

options.text: Perform the test and ask the patient to sign an ABN after the claim is denied
options.rationale: Incorrect. The ABN must be delivered before the test is performed.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer calls up-coding and unbundling “illegal fraud” without qualification. The OIG guidance says intentional or knowing upcoding could violate the False Claims Act, and the Act requires knowing conduct (including deliberate ignorance or reckless disregard, without proof of intent to defraud); the NCCI manual treats unbundling and upcoding as improper coding. The lesson teaches them as improper coding that creates False Claims Act liability when the false claim is submitted knowingly.

The reviewer’s Trap 6 dodge says the lab must give an ABN whenever Medicare may deny. CMS and the OIG add that the notice must name the specific test and the reason, be given before the service with time to decide, and must not be routine or blank; no ABN is required in emergencies. The lesson teaches the fuller rule.

CPT/HCPCS, NCCI, the False Claims Act, Medicare medical-necessity rules and the ABN are US-specific. Philippine billing and PhilHealth rules are not covered (see register flag rv-us-centric); MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
